prompt: Monthly data for a beach town show a strong positive correlation ($r = 0.9$) between ice cream sales and the number of drownings. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.label: Eating ice cream causes drownings, so sales should be limited
Drownings cause people to buy more ice cream
A lurking variable such as hot weather likely drives both, so no causal claim is justified
The correlation must be a mistake, because the two variables are unrelated

hint: A strong correlation from observational data describes a pattern. It does not say WHY the pattern exists.

hints.text: A strong correlation from observational data describes a pattern. It does not say WHY the pattern exists.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: shoe size and reading level are strongly correlated among children. Neither causes the other; age drives both. Look for the same kind of hidden variable here.
What changes month to month that would push BOTH ice cream sales and swimming (and so drownings) up at the same time?
Hot summer weather raises both. The correlation is real but not causal: choice C.

explanation: These are observational data: nobody assigned towns to eat more ice cream. So correlation alone cannot establish cause and effect.
A lurking variable, hot weather, increases ice cream sales AND sends more people swimming, which raises drownings. That explains the strong $r$ without either variable causing the other.
Choice C is the only justified conclusion. Choice D is wrong because the correlation is genuine; it is the causal story that is missing.

alternativeExplanations.title: How you could test causation
steps: Only a randomized experiment can establish cause: randomly assign beachgoers to eat ice cream or not and compare outcomes.
That is impossible and unethical here, so we are stuck with observational data and must be careful with our words.
The AP phrasing: "there is a strong positive association, but this does not imply causation."

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice D
steps: It is tempting to dismiss a surprising correlation as an error.
But $r = 0.9$ computed correctly is a real feature of the data: the months really do move together.
The surprise disappears once you spot the common cause, which is the point of choice C.
